title: The One Move of Leaving Thought
author: Annotated by Zhanran
excerpt: (From the Dream Journey Collection: Instruction for the Chan Practitioner Liaoxin Hai)

inline.s: Instruction for the Chan Practitioner Liaoxin Hai)
Only, within thought after thought, look into the place where thought has not yet arisen.

[We who have left home do so solely for the great matter of birth and death. Traveling on foot, visiting teachers and friends, is only for the sake of deciding upon the upward road for oneself; if it is not understood, one does not stop. Therefore good spiritual friends show people only this matter. In recent times the Dharma-gate has grown desolate, and this spirit is rarely heard of in any quarter; wherever one travels, there is only the air of rice-gruel and food. The old man was dwelling at the aranya on Linghu when the Chan practitioner Liaoxin came to pay his respects. On entering the gate, I saw that he had the handle of a patch-robed monk and did not seem to be an ordinary rice-and-gruel fellow. Now that he is about to return to Funiu, he burns incense and asks for instruction.]

We have left home solely for the great matter of birth and death. Wandering in the four directions, visiting teachers and friends, is only for the sake of finding the road of seeing one's own mind and nature; if one does not find it, one will not stop. Therefore good spiritual friends also instruct students only in this matter (the road of seeing the mind and nature). In recent times the Dharma-gate has grown desolate, and this spirit is rarely heard of in any quarter (seldom does one hear of good spiritual friends instructing students in the road of seeing the mind and nature). Wherever one travels, there is only the air of rice-gruel and food. The old man was dwelling at the aranya on Linghu when the Chan practitioner Liaoxin came to pay his respects. On entering the gate, I saw that he had the handle of a patch-robed monk and did not seem to be an ordinary rice-and-gruel fellow. Now that he is about to return to Funiu Mountain, he burns incense and asks for instruction.

[Handle] That which can be grasped. [Rice-and-gruel fellow] One who merely eats gruel and rice without practicing earnestly. It is said: 'When Attendant Lu entered the monks' hall, he asked: of so many masters and monks, are they monks who eat gruel and rice, or monks who investigate Chan?' (Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Lingyou of Weishan, Tanzhou) [Burn incense] To light incense.

[The old man instructed him, saying: Among the Chan communities within the sea today, the foremost is the ascetic practice of Funiu Mountain, which none of the other quarters can match. A student of the Way, if he can risk and cast away body and life, will surely not pass this lifetime in vain. But in daily practice, the most meticulous and unbroken method is to raise a single huatou (meditative phrase) with one-pointed attention. The reason one fails to transcend and attain great freedom is that one has all along clung rigidly to the huatou, never letting go of a single thought. One does not realize that in investigating Chan, one must first inwardly relinquish body and mind and outwardly abandon the world — the single move of departing from thought. Thus clinging to thought is instead being bound by thought, and one cannot attain the ground of great freedom and transcendence.]

The old man instructed, saying: Among the Chan communities within the sea today, fortunately there is the ascetic practice of Funiu Mountain, which the Chan communities of other places cannot match. A student of the Way, if he can risk and cast away body and life, will surely not pass this lifetime in vain. However, in daily practice, raising a single huatou with one-pointed attention is the most meticulous and unbroken method. The reason one fails to transcend and attain great freedom is that one has all along clung rigidly to the huatou, never letting go of a single thought. One does not realize that in investigating Chan one must first inwardly relinquish body and mind and outwardly abandon the world, and work on the single move of departing from thought. Thus clinging to thought is instead being bound by thought, and one cannot attain the ground of great freedom and transcendence.

[This time the Chan practitioner enters the mountain, and fortunately relies on the support of the rules and the assembly, and can rightly apply himself with effort right there. Only, within thought after thought,
look into the place where thought has not yet arisen
. Working on the single move of departing from thought, after a long while, suddenly the thought is snapped through, and mind and objects are both forgotten
, and like a lion loosed from its rope, one roams freely. When next you see the old man, you will surely not be the same as today in the movement and stillness of your brow and eyes.]

This time the Chan practitioner returns to Funiu Mountain, and fortunately can rely on the ascetic rules of Funiu Mountain and the ascetic assembly to temper himself, and can rightly apply himself with effort right there. Only, within thought after thought, look into the place where thought has not yet arisen. Because one is working on the single move of departing from thought, after a long while
(with only the single thought of looking remaining)

is snapped through, and mind and objects are both extinguished, and like a lion loosed from its rope, one roams freely. When next you see the old man, you will surely no longer be like the present, with no master over your movement and stillness.

[Rules and measures] Compass, square, and inked line — a metaphor for standards and discipline. [Mind and objects both forgotten ('forgotten' meaning 'extinguished')] Mind and objects both extinguished. This is the state in which both subject and object are extinguished — the mind that looks and the objects it looks at are obliterated together, which is precisely the state of seeing one's own mind and nature.
